title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
content:
Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
- Published
A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.
Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex.
However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.
A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.
"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."
- What is the new AI supercomputer planned for Essex? 
  - Published18 September 2025
The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.
But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday, external, Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.
"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.
Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.
The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.
Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.

report.summary: Microsoft has ended its funding role in Nscale’s planned £2bn Essex AI data centre, but Nscale says the project continues despite power-grid delays.
report.background: The Loughton project reflects a broader race to build AI compute in the UK, where demand for GPU capacity is rising faster than power infrastructure can be delivered. Nscale announced a £2bn facility in Essex and Microsoft initially agreed to fund a supercomputer there, part of a $30bn UK investment package. But AI data centres are extremely power-hungry, and grid connections in London and the South East are congested. The article says the site’s power supply slipped from end-2025 to the 2030s, prompting Nscale to seek alternative power sources. Microsoft’s exit from this specific commitment does not necessarily signal a UK retreat, since it continues other projects with Nscale abroad and has broad UK spending plans. Still, the episode highlights how energy availability, not just chip supply or capital, is becoming a critical bottleneck for AI infrastructure.
key_points: Microsoft has terminated its involvement in funding the supercomputer planned for Nscale’s Loughton, Essex site, according to the BBC. Microsoft declined to comment. Nscale said its relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term and that they continue working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.

The Loughton data centre was due to receive power at the end of the year, but Nscale has been told the connection will not arrive until the 2030s because of a London-wide grid issue. Nscale says it is exploring alternative power sources and other UK expansion sites.

Nscale insists it remains committed to the £2bn Loughton project and the UK. The site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it opens, and Nscale says the grid problem has no impact on its other contracts. The company is positioning the delay as site-specific rather than a broader setback.

The withdrawal comes only last month after Microsoft said some of its $30bn UK investment would fund the Loughton supercomputer. The quick reversal underscores how power-delivery risk can alter Big Tech’s AI infrastructure commitments, even when national investment plans remain intact.
report.impact: The episode shows that grid capacity is now a first-order constraint on AI expansion. For the AI industry, it may cool expectations for UK-based compute and push operators toward sites with faster power access, on-site generation, or overseas alternatives. For developers, delayed UK GPU capacity could mean continued reliance on cloud regions in Ireland, Europe, or the US; startups should avoid assuming local capacity will arrive on schedule. For regular users, the near-term effect is limited, but slower data-centre buildout could affect latency, pricing, and availability of UK-hosted AI services. Microsoft’s broader $30bn UK plan and Nscale’s other projects suggest the retreat is project-specific, not a full UK pullback.
report.tools: To follow the story, track Nscale’s project announcements, Microsoft’s UK investment updates, and UK grid-connection data from the National Energy System Operator. Open-source and public resources include Electricity Maps for grid demand and carbon data, OpenStreetMap for mapping data-centre sites, and the IEA’s data-centre energy reports. For AI infrastructure watchers, cloud-region status pages and GPU price trackers can help gauge whether UK capacity delays affect availability.
